summary.text: A finite check shows that for every \(1\le d\le2025\) there are primes \(p,q<18\) with different final digits, \(pq\le150\), and neither dividing \(d\). Thus \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\), so some \(0\le i<pq\le150\) has \(pq\mid a+id\); that term has prime divisors ending in different digits and therefore cannot satisfy the required condition.

full_proof.text:
We prove that the asserted arithmetic progression cannot exist.

Call a positive integer lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same residue modulo \(10\). Thus, if a nonzero integer is divisible by two primes having different final decimal digits, it is not lopsided.

The key observation is the following lemma about every possible common difference.

**Lemma.** If \(1\le d\le 2025\), then there are primes \(p,q<18\) such that
\[
pq\le 150,\qquad p\not\mid d,\qquad q\not\mid d,
\]
and \(p\not\equiv q\pmod {10}\).

**Proof of the lemma.** Consider the seven primes
\[
P=\{2,3,5,7,11,13,17\}.
\]
Join two primes in this set when their final decimal digits differ and their product is at most \(150\). The joined pairs are exactly
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &(2,3),(2,5),(2,7),(2,11),(2,13),(2,17),\\
 &(3,5),(3,7),(3,11),(3,17),\\
 &(5,7),(5,11),(5,13),(5,17),\\
 &(7,11),(7,13),\\
 &(11,13).
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, this follows immediately by comparing the residues
\[
2,3,5,7,1,3,7\pmod {10}
\]
of the seven primes and their pairwise products. For example, \(3\) and \(13\), as well as \(7\) and \(17\), have equal final digits; while \(11\cdot17=187\) and \(13\cdot17=221\) exceed \(150\).

Let
\[
N=\{r\in P:r\nmid d\}.
\]
Suppose, contrary to the lemma, that no joined pair has both endpoints in \(N\). Then \(N\) is an independent set in the graph just described.

Every independent set is contained in one of the following six maximal independent sets:
\[
\{2\},\quad \{5\},\quad \{3,13\},\quad \{7,17\},
\quad \{11,17\},\quad \{13,17\}.
\]
Here is a direct check of this classification. The prime \(2\) is joined to every other vertex, so an independent set containing \(2\) is contained in \(\{2\}\). The same is true of \(5\). After removing \(2\) and \(5\), if an independent set contains \(3\), then the only other possible vertex is \(13\), giving \(\{3,13\}\). If it contains \(7\), its only possible companion is \(17\), giving \(\{7,17\}\). If it contains \(11\), its only possible companion is \(17\), giving \(\{11,17\}\). Finally, if it contains neither \(3,7,11\), it is contained in \(\{13,17\}\). This also covers the empty and singleton independent sets.

Choose one of these six sets \(I\) containing \(N\). Every prime in \(P\setminus I\) lies outside \(N\), and therefore divides \(d\). Since these are distinct primes, their product divides \(d\). The six possibilities give the following table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
I& P\setminus I&\displaystyle\prod_{r\in P\setminus I}r\\ \hline
\{2\}&\{3,5,7,11,13,17\}&255255\\
\{5\}&\{2,3,7,11,13,17\}&102102\\
\{3,13\}&\{2,5,7,11,17\}&13090\\
\{7,17\}&\{2,3,5,11,13\}&4290\\
\{11,17\}&\{2,3,5,7,13\}&2730\\
\{13,17\}&\{2,3,5,7,11\}&2310.
\end{array}
\]
In every case a positive integer greater than \(2025\) divides \(d\). A positive divisor of \(d\) cannot exceed \(d\), so this contradicts \(d\le2025\). Hence \(N\) must contain a joined pair \(p,q\), and that pair has all the properties asserted in the lemma. \(\square\)

Now suppose for contradiction that there are integers \(a,d\) satisfying
\[
a\ge2,\qquad 1\le d\le2025,
\]
such that all \(150\) terms
\[
a,
\ a+d,
\ a+2d,
\ldots,
\ a+149d
\]
are lopsided.

Apply the lemma to \(d\), obtaining primes \(p,q\) with different final digits such that
\[
pq\le150,
\qquad p\nmid d,
\qquad q\nmid d.
\]
Because \(p\) is prime and does not divide \(d\), \(\gcd(d,p)=1\); similarly \(\gcd(d,q)=1\). Also, the different residues of \(p\) and \(q\) modulo \(10\) imply in particular that \(p\ne q\). Hence \(p\) and \(q\) are coprime, and consequently
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]

Set \(m=pq\). Since \(d\) is invertible modulo \(m\), the congruence
\[
a+id\equiv0\pmod m
\]
has a solution. Explicitly, Bezout's identity supplies integers \(u,v\) with
\[
ud+vm=1.
\]
Choose \(i\) to be the least nonnegative residue of \(-au\) modulo \(m\). Then
\[
0\le i<m
\]
and, modulo \(m\),
\[
a+id\equiv a+(-au)d=a(1-ud)\equiv0,
\]
because \(ud\equiv1\pmod m\). Therefore
\[
pq=m\mid a+id.
\]
Moreover, \(m=pq\le150\), so
\[
0\le i<m\le150,
\]
which implies \(0\le i<150\). Thus \(a+id\) is one of the alleged \(150\) lopsided terms.

Since \(pq\mid a+id\), both \(p\) and \(q\) divide \(a+id\). The number \(a+id\) is positive—in fact it is at least \(a\ge2\)—so these primes genuinely occur among its prime divisors. But \(p\) and \(q\) have different residues modulo \(10\). Hence the prime divisors of \(a+id\) do not all share one final decimal digit, and \(a+id\) is not lopsided. This contradicts the assumption that every term with index \(0\le i<150\) is lopsided.

Therefore there do not exist integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) for which all \(150\) numbers \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\), occur in A381159. The conjectured progression does not exist.
